scenes.spoken: Qadamar decides, on every request, who may see or do what. And it keeps a record of every decision.
Think of each request as a marble. It passes a row of gates, always in the same order. A single no is enough to stop it.
First case: a payment. Whoever created it can neither approve it nor release it. A second person has to.

In an emergency, you can break the glass. Access lasts four hours at most, never for yourself, an alert goes out, and someone else reviews it afterwards. But it never grants a clearance level you don't already hold.
Documents carry a level, from L zero to L three. You cannot read above your level. And you cannot write below it, so a secret never leaks downwards.
Context is checked on every request: network, time, device, recent sign-in. Off the trusted network, the reachable level drops. And if a signal is missing, the answer is no.
To change a rule, you first see its impact: who gains access, and who loses it. Then a second person approves. Nobody can approve their own change.
Every decision is written to a chained log. If one entry is altered, the chain breaks, and verification shows it.
Your access rules in one place, instead of scattered through the code. Qadamar.
